name: Proverbs
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (Old Greek) through Brenton’s public-domain English translation. The Greek Proverbs differs from the Hebrew more than most books. It contains many extra lines not found in the Hebrew (for example after 3:16, 4:27, 6:8, 9:12, and 9:18), and a few Hebrew lines are missing from it; the more significant differences are footnoted. In chapters 24–31 the Greek also arranges the material in a different order: 30:1–14 follows 24:22; 30:15–33 and 31:1–9 follow 24:34; chapters 25–29 come next; and the poem of 31:10–31 closes the book. This translation keeps the Hebrew order. In quotations from the Septuagint, “the Lord” stands for the Greek kyrios, its usual substitute for the name Yahweh. Wisdom is personified as a woman in chapters 1–9, and the feminine pronouns of the Hebrew are kept. The poem of 31:10–31 is an alphabetic acrostic; the Hebrew letter of each verse is given in the notes. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible, which here matches the Hebrew.

verses.text: The proverbs{a} of Solomon{b} son of David,{c} king of Israel:{d}

for gaining wisdom and discipline,
for grasping words of insight;

for taking in the discipline of good sense,
righteousness, justice, and fairness;

for giving shrewdness to the naive,
knowledge and discretion to the young.

The wise who hear will increase in learning,
and the discerning will acquire skill in steering,

for understanding a proverb and a figure,
the words of the wise and their riddles.

The fear of Yahweh is where knowledge begins;{e}
wisdom and discipline the foolish scorn.{f}

Listen, my son, to your father’s discipline,
and do not abandon your mother’s teaching,{g}

for they will be a lovely garland on your head
and a pendant around your neck.

My son, if sinners entice you,
do not give in.

like Sheol,{h} let us gulp them down alive,
entire, like those descending to the Pit;

we will find all kinds of precious goods
and fill our houses with plunder.

Cast your lot in among us;
one money bag for us all”;

my son, do not walk on the road with them;
keep your foot from their path,

for their feet run to evil
and hurry to shed blood.

For in vain a net is spread out
while any winged creature is watching!{i}

Yet these men lie in wait for their own blood;
they ambush their own lives.

Such are the ways of everyone greedy for gain:
it takes away the life of those who possess it.

Wisdom{j} shouts in the open air;
in the public squares she lifts her voice.

At the head of the noisy streets she calls out;
at the openings of the city gates she makes her speech:

“How long, you naive ones, will you love naivety,
and mockers delight in mocking,
and fools hate knowledge?

Because I called and you refused,
I stretched out my hand and no one paid attention,

because you brushed aside all my advice
and wanted nothing of my reproof,

I in turn will laugh at your disaster;
I will mock when dread comes on you,

when dread comes on you like a storm
and your disaster sweeps in like a whirlwind,
when distress and anguish come on you.

Then they will call me, but I will not answer;
they will look hard for me but not find me.

Because they hated knowledge
and did not choose the fear of Yahweh,

would have none of my counsel,
and spurned all my rebuke,

they will eat the fruit of their own way
and be glutted with their own schemes.

For the waywardness of the naive kills them,
and the ease of fools ruins them.

But whoever listens to me will live secure,
at ease, without dread of harm.”

notes.text: Hebrew mishle, plural of mashal, a word covering proverbs, sayings, comparisons, and parables.
Solomon, Hebrew Shelomoh, related to shalom, “peace.”
David, “beloved.”
Israel, “he strives with God” (Genesis 32:28).
Or “the first and chief part.”
The Septuagint adds “and there is good understanding for all who practice it, and reverence toward God is the beginning of perception” (compare Psalm 111:10).
Hebrew torah, “teaching” or “instruction,” the word later used for the Law.
The realm of the dead; also “the Pit” in the next line.
The meaning may be that a bird is not fooled by a trap set in plain view, unlike these men; or that the bird, seeing only the bait, flies into it anyway.

Here Wisdom (Hebrew chokhmoth, a plural form) appears as a woman calling in public, a portrait developed in chapters 8–9, where she is set opposite the “foreign woman” and Folly. The figure is often called Lady Wisdom.

verses.text:
My son, if you take in my words
and store up my commands within you,

tuning your ear to wisdom,
bending your heart toward understanding;

yes, if you call out for insight
and lift up your voice for understanding,

if you seek her like silver
and hunt for her as for hidden treasure,

then you will understand the fear of Yahweh
and find the knowledge of God.

For Yahweh is the giver of wisdom;
knowledge and understanding are the words of his mouth.

He stores up sound wisdom{a} for the upright;
he is a shield to those whose walk is blameless,

keeping watch over the tracks of justice
and protecting the road of his faithful ones.{b}

Then you will understand righteousness and justice
and fairness, every good track.

When wisdom enters your heart
and knowledge becomes a delight to your soul,

Discretion will keep watch over you;
understanding will stand guard over you,

rescuing you from the way of evil,
from men who speak perversely,

who leave the straight paths
to walk in the ways of darkness,

who delight in doing wrong
and revel in the perversity of evil,

whose paths are twisted
and whose tracks are crooked;

rescuing you also from the strange woman,{c}
from the foreign woman with her smooth talk,

who has left the companion of her youth
and forgotten the covenant of her God.{d}

For her house sinks down to death,{e}
and her paths lead to the shades of the dead.{f}

All who go in to her never return;
they do not reach the paths of life again.

Therefore follow the road of the good
and stay on the tracks of the righteous.

For the upright will dwell in the land,
and the blameless will remain in it,

but the wicked will be cut off from the land,
and the treacherous will be torn out of it.

notes.text: Hebrew tushiyyah, “sound judgment” or “success.”
Hebrew chasidim, those loyal to the covenant.
Hebrew zarah, “strange” or “outsider,” and in the next line nokhriyyah, “foreign”; in Proverbs these words describe another man’s wife, an adulteress. She appears again in 5:3–20; 6:24–35; 7:5–27.
Or “the covenant made before her God,” that is, her marriage vow.
Or “For she sinks down to death; her house…”; the Hebrew is difficult.
Hebrew repha’im, the shades, the dead in Sheol.

verses.text:
My son, do not forget my teaching;
let your heart keep my commands,

for they will add to you length of days,
years of life, and well-being.

So you will find favor and good repute
in the sight of God and of people.

Trust in Yahweh with your whole heart,
and do not lean on your own understanding.

Acknowledge him in every path you take,
and he will smooth out your roads.

Do not be wise in your own sight;
fear Yahweh and turn from evil.

It will be healing for your navel{a}
and refreshment{b} for your bones.

Give honor to Yahweh out of your riches
and out of the firstfruits of all your produce;

then your barns will be filled with plenty,
and your vats will burst with new wine.

My son, do not reject Yahweh’s discipline,
and do not resent his correction,

for Yahweh corrects the one he loves,
as a father the son in whom he delights.{c}

Happy is the person who finds wisdom,
the person who gains understanding,

for her profit is better than profit from silver,
and her yield than fine gold.

She is more precious than corals;{d}
nothing you desire can compare with her.

Long life is in her right hand;
in her left hand are riches and honor.{e}

Her ways are ways of delight,
and all her paths are peace.

She is a tree of life to those who grasp her,
and those who hold her fast are called happy.

Yahweh by wisdom founded the earth;
by understanding he set the heavens in place.

By his knowledge the depths burst open,
and the clouds drip down dew.

My son, do not let them slip from your sight;
keep sound wisdom and discretion.

They will be life for your soul
and grace for your neck.

Then you will go your way safely,
and your foot will not trip.

When you lie down, you will have no fear;
you will lie down, and your sleep will be sweet.{f}

Do not fear sudden terror
or the ruin of the wicked when it comes,

for Yahweh will be your confidence
and will keep your foot from the snare.

Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due,
when it is in your power to act.

Do not tell your neighbor, “Go away, come back later,
tomorrow I will give it,” when it is right there with you.

Do not devise evil against your neighbor
when he lives in trust beside you.

Do not quarrel with anyone for no reason
when he has done you no harm.

Do not be jealous of a man of violence,
and do not choose a single one of his ways,

for the devious are detestable to Yahweh,
but the upright are in his confidence.

Yahweh’s curse is on the house of the wicked,
but he blesses the home of the righteous.

Toward mockers he is a mocker,
but to the humble he shows favor.{g}

The wise will inherit honor,
but fools carry off disgrace.{h}

notes.text: Or “your body”; the Septuagint reads “your body.”
Literally “drink” or “moistening.”
The Septuagint reads “and he scourges every son whom he receives,” the form quoted in Hebrews 12:6.
Or “rubies” or “pearls”; the exact gem is uncertain.
The Septuagint adds “Out of her mouth comes righteousness, and she carries law and mercy on her tongue.”
The Septuagint reads “If you rest, you will be unafraid; if you sleep, you will sleep sweetly.”
The Septuagint reads “The Lord opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Greek kyrios, its usual rendering of Yahweh), the form quoted in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.
Or “but fools exalt disgrace”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text:
Listen, children, to a father’s discipline;
pay attention so as to learn understanding.

It is sound learning I hand on to you;
do not walk away from my instruction.

I too was once a boy in my father’s house,
young and tender, my mother’s only one,

Get wisdom, get understanding;
do not forget, do not swerve from the words of my mouth.

Do not leave her, and she will guard you;
love her, and she will keep you safe.

The beginning of wisdom is: get wisdom!
With all you have gotten, get understanding.{a}

Prize her, and she will lift you high;
she will bring you honor if you embrace her.

She will set a graceful garland on your head;
a crown of splendor she will hand to you.”

Hear, my son, and accept my sayings,
and the years of your life will be many.

I have taught you the way of wisdom;
I have led you along upright tracks.

When you walk, your stride will not be hampered,
and if you run, you will not stumble.

Seize hold of discipline and never loosen your grip;
protect her, since she is your very life.

Do not set foot on the path of the wicked,
and do not stride along the way of evildoers.

Avoid it, do not cross over to it;
turn away from it and pass on.

For they cannot sleep unless they have done wrong;
their sleep is snatched away unless they have tripped someone up.

For they eat the bread of wickedness
and drink the wine of violence.

The road of the righteous is like first light at daybreak,
glowing ever stronger until the day is full.

The road of the wicked is like thick gloom;
they cannot tell what trips them up.

My son, attend to my words;
bend your ear to my sayings.

Do not let them slip from your eyes;
keep them in the center of your heart.

For they are life to those who find them
and healing to all their flesh.

More than anything you guard, guard your heart,
for from it flow the springs of life.

Put crooked speech away from you;
keep devious lips far from you.

Let your eyes look straight ahead,
your gaze be fixed directly before you.

Make a level path for your feet to travel,
and every road you take will hold firm.

Lean neither right nor left;
keep your foot back from evil.{b}

notes.text: This verse is not in the Septuagint.
The Septuagint adds “For God knows the ways on the right, but those on the left are crooked; and he will make your ways straight and guide your steps in peace.”

verses.text:
My son, attend to my wisdom;
bend your ear to my understanding,

so that discretion stays with you
and your lips preserve knowledge.

For the lips of the strange woman drip honey,
and her palate is smoother than oil,

but in the end she is bitter as wormwood,{a}
sharp as a two-edged sword.

Her feet go down to death;
her steps take hold of Sheol.

She does not keep straight on the path of life;
her tracks wander, and she does not know it.{b}

So now, children, listen to me,
and do not turn aside from the words of my mouth.

Keep your path well away from her;
stay clear of the entrance to her house,

lest you hand over your prime to other men
and your years to a merciless one;

strangers will feast on your strength,
and your labors will go to a foreigner’s house.

You will moan when your end comes,
when your flesh and your body are wasted,

and you will say, “Oh, how I loathed discipline!
How my heart despised reproof!

I would not listen to the voice of my teachers
or bend my ear to my instructors.

I came close to utter ruin
in the midst of the assembly and congregation.”

Draw your water from a cistern that is yours,
running water out of a well that is yours.{c}

Must your springs spill out into the streets,
your channels of water into the squares?

Let them be yours alone,
not shared with strangers.

May your fountain be blessed,
and rejoice in the wife of your youth,

Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a strange woman
and embrace the bosom of a foreigner?

For a man’s ways are in full view of Yahweh,
and he weighs{d} all his paths.

The wicked man’s own iniquities will trap him;
he will be held fast in the cords of his sin.

He will die for lack of discipline,
and through the greatness of his folly he will stagger away.{e}

notes.text: Wormwood, a plant with a very bitter taste, a byword for bitterness.
Or “so that you do not walk the level path of life; her tracks wander, and you do not know it.”
In verses 15–18 water, cistern, and fountain are images of the man’s own wife.
Or “levels.”
The Hebrew word for “stagger” is the same as “be intoxicated” in verses 19–20.

verses.text:
My son, if you have stood surety for your neighbor,
have struck hands in pledge for a stranger,

if you are snared by the words of your mouth,
caught by what your own lips have said,

then do this, my son, and get yourself free,
since you have fallen into your neighbor’s hand:
go, humble yourself,{a} and pester your neighbor.

Do not let your eyes close in sleep
or your eyelids droop.

Tear yourself loose like a gazelle from the hunter’s grip,{b}
like a bird from the fowler’s hand.

Go to the ant, you lazybones;
watch her ways and grow wise.

She has no commander,
no overseer or ruler,

yet she lays in her food in summer
and gathers her provisions at harvest.{c}

How long will you lie there, lazybones?
When will you get up from your sleep?

A little sleep, a little dozing,
a little folding of the hands to rest,

and poverty will come on you like a prowler,
and want like an armed man.{d}

A good-for-nothing,{e} a man of iniquity,
walks around with crooked speech,

winking with his eyes, signaling with his feet,
pointing with his fingers.

Perversity is in his heart; he devises evil all the time;
he lets loose quarrels.

Therefore disaster will come on him suddenly;
in an instant he will be broken beyond healing.

There are six things Yahweh hates,
seven that are detestable to him:{f}

haughty eyes, a lying tongue,
hands that shed innocent blood,

a heart that devises wicked schemes,
feet quick to run to evil,

a lying witness who puffs out falsehoods,
and one who stirs up strife between brothers.

My son, keep your father’s command,
and do not abandon your mother’s teaching.

Fasten them to your heart forever;
knot them about your throat.

For the command is a lamp, the teaching is light,
and correction that disciplines is the road to life,

keeping you from the wicked woman,{g}
from the slick tongue of the outsider.

Do not let your heart crave her loveliness,
and do not be taken in by the flutter of her lashes.

For a prostitute’s price is a round of bread,
but another man’s wife stalks a man’s very life.{h}

Can a man scoop fire into his lap
and his clothes not be burned?

Or can one walk on hot coals
and his feet not be scorched?

So it is with one who goes in to his neighbor’s wife;
no one who touches her will go unpunished.

People do not despise a thief if he steals
to fill his belly when he is hungry;

yet if caught, he must repay sevenfold;
he must give up all the goods of his house.

The man who commits adultery has no sense;
he who does so brings ruin on himself.

Blows and dishonor he will get,
and his disgrace will not be wiped away.

For jealousy kindles a husband’s rage;
on the day of vengeance he will not spare.

He will accept no compensation;
he will not be appeased though you multiply gifts.

notes.text: Or “trample yourself,” that is, swallow your pride.
Literally “from the hand”; “of the hunter” is supplied from the parallel line, as in some ancient witnesses.

The Septuagint adds “Or go to the bee and learn how diligent she is and how earnest her work is; kings and commoners use her labors for health, and she is desired and honored by all; though weak in strength, she is advanced because she honors wisdom.”
The Septuagint adds “But if you are diligent, your harvest will come like a spring, and poverty will run away like a poor runner.”
Hebrew ’adam beliyya‘al, “a man of Belial,” a word for worthlessness or wickedness.
A “six… seven” saying, a numerical pattern also found in 30:15–31.
The Septuagint reads “from the married woman.”
Or “For on account of a prostitute a man is brought to a loaf of bread.” The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.

verses.text:
My son, keep my words
and treasure up my commands within you.{a}

Keep my commands and live,
my teaching like the pupil of your eye.

Tie them on your fingers;
inscribe them on the tablet of your heart.

Say to wisdom, “You are my sister,”
and call understanding your kinswoman,

to keep you from the strange woman,
from the foreign woman with her smooth words.

From the window of my house
I looked out through my lattice,

and I saw among the naive,
I noticed among the youths,
a young man lacking sense,

passing along the street near her corner,
taking the road toward her house,

in the twilight, in the evening of the day,
in the dead of night and the dark.

And there a woman comes to meet him,
dressed like a prostitute, with a guarded heart.{b}

She is loud and unruly;
her feet never stay at home;

one moment out in the road, the next in the market squares,
at every street corner she waits in ambush.

She seizes him and kisses him;
boldfaced, she tells him,

“I had to offer peace offerings;
today I have paid my vows.{c}

So I have come out on purpose to meet you,
searching for your face, and here you are!

I have spread my couch with coverings,
colored linens from Egypt.

I have sprinkled my bed
with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.

Come, let us soak ourselves in lovemaking till dawn;
let us revel in love.

For my husband is not at home;
he has gone on a long journey.

He took a bag of money with him;
he will come home at the full moon.”

With her many persuasions she bends him;
with her smooth lips she drives him on.

until an arrow pierces his liver,
like a bird rushing into a snare,
not knowing it will cost him his life.

So now, children, listen to me;
pay attention to the words of my mouth.

Let your heart not veer toward her roads;
do not stray onto her tracks,

for many are the victims she has brought down,
and countless are all those she has slain.

Her house is the way to Sheol,
going down to the chambers of death.

notes.text: The Septuagint adds “My son, honor the Lord, and you will be strong; and besides him fear no one.”
Or “with secret intent” or “with a veiled heart.”
The meat of a peace offering had to be eaten within a day or two (Leviticus 7:15–16), so she has a feast ready.
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain; the Septuagint reads “as a dog to bonds, or as a deer shot in the liver with an arrow.”

verses.text:
Listen! Is that not Wisdom calling,
Understanding lifting up her voice?{a}

On the heights beside the road,
where the paths meet, she takes her stand;

beside the gates at the entrance to the city,
at the doorways she cries aloud:

“To you, people, I am calling;
my voice goes out to all humankind.

You naive, learn shrewdness;
you fools, learn sense.{b}

Listen, for I speak of noble things;
from my lips come upright words.

My mouth utters truth;
wickedness is detestable to my lips.

All the words of my mouth are in righteousness;
nothing in them is twisted or crooked.

They are all plain to the discerning
and right to those who find knowledge.

Take my discipline instead of silver,
knowledge rather than choice gold,

for wisdom is better than corals,
and nothing desirable can equal her.

I, Wisdom, live with shrewdness;
I find out knowledge and discretion.

To fear Yahweh is to hate evil.
Pride and arrogance, the way of evil,
and a perverse mouth I hate.

Counsel and sound wisdom are mine;
I am understanding; strength is mine.

Through me kings hold their thrones
and rulers enact just laws.

By me princes govern,
and nobles, all who judge rightly.{c}

Those who love me I love,
and those who seek me early will find me.

Riches and honor are with me,
enduring wealth and righteousness.

My fruit is better than gold, than pure gold,
and my yield than choice silver.

In the road of righteousness I go,
in the middle of the tracks of justice,

to endow with wealth those who love me
and to fill their treasuries.{d}

Yahweh acquired me{e} at the beginning of his way,
before his works of long ago.

From everlasting I was set up,{f}
from the first, before the earth began.

When there were no depths I was brought forth,
when there were no springs heavy with water.

Before the mountains were sunk in place,
before the hills, I was brought forth,

while he had not yet made the earth and the open fields
or the first of the dust of the world.

When he set the heavens in place, I was there,
when he drew a circle on the face of the deep,

when he made firm the clouds above,
when the springs of the deep grew strong,

when he assigned the sea its limit
so that the waters would not pass his command,
when he marked out the foundations of the earth,

laughing over the world, his earth,
and finding my joy among humankind.

Now then, children, hear me:
blessed are those who keep to my ways.

Listen to discipline and be wise;
do not neglect it.

Blessed is the person who hears me,
keeping watch at my gates day by day,
standing guard at my doorposts.

For whoever finds me finds life
and obtains favor from Yahweh,

but whoever fails to find me wrongs his own soul;{h}
all who hate me are in love with death.”

notes.text: Wisdom speaks in her own voice through this chapter. On the figure of Lady Wisdom, see the note at 1:20.
Literally “understand heart.”
Literally “all the judges of righteousness”; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read “the earth.”
The Septuagint adds “If I tell you what happens daily, I will remember to recount the things of old.”

Hebrew qanani, from qanah, which usually means “acquire,” “get,” or “possess” (as in 4:5, 7), and in a few places may mean “create” or “beget” (Genesis 14:19, 22; Deuteronomy 32:6). The Septuagint has ektisen, “created” (Brenton “made”); Aquila and other later Greek versions have “acquired” or “possessed.” The verse became central in the fourth-century debates over the nature of Christ, identified with Wisdom.
Or “woven,” as in Psalm 139:13, or “installed.”
Hebrew ’amon; or “like a little child,” reading ’amun, “nursling.” The Septuagint has “suiting myself to him.”
Or “whoever sins against me.”

verses.text:
Wisdom has built her house;
she has hewn out her seven pillars.{a}

She has slaughtered her animals, mixed her wine,
and set her table.

She has sent out her young women; she calls
from the highest points of the city:

“Whoever is naive, turn in here!”
To the one lacking sense she says,

“Come, eat of my bread
and drink of the wine I have mixed.

Leave naivety behind and live;
walk straight on in the way of understanding.”

Whoever corrects a mocker earns abuse;
whoever rebukes a wicked man gets hurt.

Do not rebuke a mocker, or he will hate you;
rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.

Instruct the wise, and they grow wiser still;
teach the righteous, and they add to their learning.

The fear of Yahweh is the start of wisdom,
and knowledge of the Holy One{b} is understanding.{c}

For through me your days will multiply,
and years of life will be added to you.

If you are wise, you are wise to your own benefit;
if you mock, you alone will bear it.{d}

Lady Folly is boisterous,
naive, and knows nothing at all.{e}

She sits at the door of her house,
on a seat at the heights of the city,

hailing the passers-by
who are keeping to the straight road:

“Whoever is naive, turn in here!”
To the one lacking sense she says,

“Stolen water is sweet,
and bread eaten in secret is delicious.”

But he does not know that the shades are there,
that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.{f}

notes.text: The seven pillars may picture a grand house, the seven days of creation, or the completeness of Wisdom’s work; the meaning is debated.
Hebrew qedoshim, plural, perhaps a plural of majesty; or “of holy ones.”
The Septuagint adds “for to know the law is the mark of a sound mind.”

The Septuagint adds three verses comparing the one who leans on lies to someone who herds the winds and chases birds in flight, abandons his own vineyard, and walks through a dry desert gathering barrenness with his hands.

Literally “A woman of folly.” Folly is drawn as Wisdom’s rival, inviting the same naive guests (compare verses 4 and 16). The second line is uncertain; the Septuagint reads “and she does not know shame.”

The Septuagint adds “But hurry away; do not linger in the place or fix your eye on her, for so you will pass through strange water. Keep away from strange water, and do not drink from a strange fountain, so that you may live long and years of life may be added to you.”

verses.text:
Treasures gained by wickedness bring no profit,
but righteousness rescues from death.

Yahweh will not let the righteous go hungry,
but he pushes away the craving of the wicked.

A slack hand brings poverty,
but the hand of the diligent makes rich.{b}

A son who gathers in summer acts wisely;
a son who sleeps through harvest brings shame.

Blessings rest on the head of the righteous,
but the mouth of the wicked hides violence.{c}

To remember the righteous is to bless them,
but the name of the wicked decays.

The wise of heart takes commands to heart,
but a babbling fool will be thrown down.

Whoever walks in integrity walks securely,
but whoever twists his ways will be found out.

One who winks the eye causes grief,
and a babbling fool will be thrown down.{d}

The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life,
but the mouth of the wicked hides violence.

Hatred stirs up quarrels,
but love throws a covering over every offense.

Wisdom is found on the lips of the discerning,
but a rod is for the back of the one without sense.

The wise store up knowledge,
but the mouth of a fool brings ruin near.

The wealth of the rich is their fortified city;
the ruin of the poor is their poverty.

The wages of the righteous lead to life,
the income of the wicked to sin.

One who heeds discipline is on the path to life,
but one who ignores correction leads others astray.

Lips that cover up hatred are liars,
and the one who puts out slander is a fool.

When words are many, wrongdoing is not lacking,
but the one who holds back his lips is prudent.

The tongue of the righteous is choice silver;
the heart of the wicked is worth little.

The lips of the righteous feed many,
but fools die for lack of sense.

Yahweh’s blessing is what makes rich,
and toil adds nothing to it.{e}

Doing wrong is like a game to a fool,
and wisdom is the same to a man of understanding.

The thing the wicked man fears overtakes him;
the longing of the righteous is granted.

When the storm has passed, the wicked are gone,
but the righteous stand on an everlasting foundation.

Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes
is the sluggard to those who send him.

The fear of Yahweh lengthens days,
but the years of the wicked will be cut short.

The hope of the righteous ends in joy,
but the expectation of the wicked comes to nothing.

The way of Yahweh is a stronghold for the blameless,
but ruin for those who do evil.

Forever the righteous stays unmoved;
the wicked will not live on in the land.

The mouth of the righteous bears the fruit of wisdom,
but the perverse tongue will be cut off.

The lips of the righteous know what is pleasing,
but the mouth of the wicked, only perversity.

notes.text: Chapters 10:1–22:16 are a collection of mostly two-line sayings, 375 in number, the numerical value of the Hebrew letters in the name Solomon (shlmh).
The Septuagint adds “A son who is instructed will be wise and will use the fool as a servant.”
Or “but violence covers the mouth of the wicked”; the same line recurs in verse 11.
The second line repeats verse 8b; the Septuagint reads “but one who reproves boldly makes peace.”
Or “and he adds no sorrow with it.”

verses.text:
False scales are detestable to Yahweh,
but an honest weight is his delight.{a}

When pride comes, disgrace comes too,
but with the humble is wisdom.

The upright are led by their own wholeness;
the treacherous are ruined by their own twisting.

Wealth is no help on the day of wrath,
but righteousness rescues from death.{b}

The righteousness of the blameless makes his road straight,
but the wicked falls by his own wickedness.

Their righteousness sets the upright free,
while traitors are trapped by their greed.

When a wicked man dies, his hope perishes,
and the expectation of strength is lost.{c}

The righteous is rescued from trouble,
and the wicked comes in his place.

With his mouth the godless destroys his neighbor,
but by knowledge the righteous are rescued.

When the righteous prosper, the city rejoices,
and when the wicked perish, there are shouts of joy.

By the blessing of the upright a city is raised high,
but by the mouth of the wicked it is torn down.

To look down on a neighbor is senseless;
a discerning person holds his tongue.

A gossip goes around revealing secrets,
but the trustworthy in spirit keeps a matter covered.

Without guidance a people falls,
but with many counselors there is victory.

Whoever pledges for a stranger will suffer harm,
but whoever hates handshake pledges is secure.

A gracious woman gains honor,
and ruthless men gain riches.{d}

A kind man does good to himself,
but a cruel one harms his own flesh.

The wicked earns deceptive wages,
but one who sows righteousness gets a true reward.

Steadfast righteousness leads to life,
but whoever pursues evil goes to his death.

The crooked of heart are detestable to Yahweh,
but those whose way is blameless are his delight.

Be sure of it: the evildoer will not go unpunished,
but the offspring of the righteous will escape.

A gold ring in a pig’s snout—
so is a beautiful woman who has turned from good sense.

What the righteous long for is only good;
what the wicked can expect is wrath.

One gives freely and grows richer;
another holds back more than is right and ends in want.

The person who blesses others will grow fat,
and the one who gives drink will be given drink.

People curse the one who hoards grain,
but blessing crowns the head of the one who sells it.

The one who looks hard for good is looking for favor;
the one who hunts for evil, it will find him.

Whoever trusts in his riches will fall,
but the righteous will flourish like green leaves.

A man who brings trouble on his own house will be left holding the wind,
and the fool ends up slave to the wise.

The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life,
and a wise person wins lives.{e}

If on earth the righteous get their due,
all the more the wicked and the sinner!{f}

notes.text: Literally “a full stone”; weights were stones carried in a merchant’s bag.
The Septuagint lacks this verse.
Or “of wealth”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
The Septuagint expands this verse: “A gracious wife brings glory to her husband, but a woman who hates righteousness is a seat of dishonor. The lazy come to want, but the diligent hold on to wealth.”
Or “takes lives.” The Septuagint reads “but the lives of transgressors are cut off before their time.”
The Septuagint reads “If the righteous are scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” quoted in 1 Peter 4:18.

verses.text:
To love correction is to love knowledge;
to hate reproof is brutish.

A good person obtains favor from Yahweh,
but a man of schemes he condemns.

No one is made secure by wickedness,
but the root of the righteous will not be moved.

A woman of strength is her husband’s crown,
but one who shames him is like rot in his bones.

The plans of the righteous are just;
the guidance of the wicked is deceit.

The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood,
but the mouth of the upright rescues them.

Overthrow the wicked and they are no more,
but the house of the righteous will stand.

A man is praised according to his good sense,
but one with a twisted mind is despised.

Better a nobody with a servant
than a self-important man with no bread.

The righteous knows the needs of his animals,
but the compassion of the wicked is cruel.

Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread,
but whoever chases worthless things lacks sense.{a}

The wicked covets the catch of evildoers,
but the root of the righteous yields fruit.{b}

In the offense of the lips is an evil snare,
but the righteous escapes from trouble.{c}

From the fruit of his mouth a person is filled with good,
and the work of his hands comes back to him.

The way of a fool is right in his own eyes,
but the wise listens to advice.

A fool shows his anger at once,
but the shrewd ignores an insult.

A truthful witness declares what is just,
and a lying witness, what deceives.

Some speak rashly, like the thrusts of a sword,
but the tongue of the wise brings healing.

Truthful lips endure forever,
but a lying tongue lasts only a moment.

Treachery lives in the heart of evil schemers,
while counselors of peace are glad.

No harm befalls the righteous,
but the wicked are filled with trouble.

Lying lips are detestable to Yahweh,
but those who act faithfully are his delight.

A shrewd man conceals knowledge,
but the heart of fools proclaims folly.

The hand of the diligent will rule,
but the slack hand will be put to forced labor.

Worry in the heart bows a man down,
and a kind word cheers him.

The righteous guides his neighbor,{d}
but the way of the wicked leads them astray.

The lazy man does not roast his game,
but a diligent man gains precious wealth.{e}

In the path of righteousness is life,
and along its way there is no death.{f}

notes.text: The Septuagint adds “Whoever enjoys himself at banquets of wine will leave dishonor in his strongholds.”
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.
The Septuagint adds “One whose looks are gentle will be pitied, but one who quarrels at the gates afflicts souls.”
Or “The righteous searches out his pasture”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.
Or “but the way of a path leads to death,” with some ancient witnesses.

verses.text:
A wise son heeds his father’s discipline,
but a mocker does not listen to rebuke.

From the fruit of his mouth a person eats good things,
but the appetite of the treacherous is for violence.

Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life;
whoever opens wide his lips comes to ruin.

The sluggard craves and gets nothing,
but the appetite of the diligent is richly satisfied.

The righteous hates a lie,
but the wicked brings stench and shame.

Righteousness keeps watch over a blameless road,
and wickedness brings the sinner down.{a}

Some put on a show of wealth and own nothing;
some put on a show of poverty and own a fortune.

A man’s riches may ransom his life,
but the poor hears no threat.

The light of the righteous shines brightly,
but the lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out.{b}

Arrogance yields nothing but quarrels,
while the well-advised have wisdom.

Money from vanity shrinks away;
money gathered by hand grows.

Long-delayed hope sickens the heart;
a longing that comes true is a tree of life.

Whoever despises a word will pay for it,
but whoever fears a command will be rewarded.{c}

The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life,
for turning away from the snares of death.

Good sense wins favor,
but the way of the treacherous is their ruin.{d}

Every shrewd person acts with knowledge,
but a fool spreads out his folly.

A wicked messenger falls into trouble,
but a faithful envoy brings healing.

Poverty and disgrace come to the one who ignores discipline,
but whoever heeds correction is honored.

Desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul,
but turning from evil is detestable to fools.

Walk with the wise and become wise,
but the companion of fools will suffer harm.

Disaster pursues sinners,
but the righteous are repaid with good.

The good leave something for their children’s children;
the sinner’s goods are laid up for the just.

The new-broken fields of the poor can grow plenty to eat,
yet some are swept away for want of justice.{e}

Whoever spares his rod hates his son,
but whoever loves him is diligent to discipline him.

The righteous eats to his heart’s content,
but the belly of the wicked goes empty.

notes.text: The Septuagint lacks this verse.
The Septuagint adds “Deceitful souls go astray in sins, but the righteous show pity and mercy.”
The Septuagint adds “A deceitful son will have nothing good, but a wise servant will prosper, and his way will be made straight.”
Or “is enduring”; the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “is in destruction.”
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.

verses.text:
Wise women build up their houses,{a}
but Folly tears hers down with her own hands.

A man who walks uprightly fears Yahweh;
a man crooked in his ways despises him.

In the fool’s mouth is a rod for his pride,{b}
but the lips of the wise keep them safe.

Where there are no oxen, the manger stays clean,
but an ox’s strength brings in a large harvest.

An honest witness does not lie,
but a false witness pours out lies.

The scoffer looks for wisdom and never finds it,
but to the discerning, knowledge comes easily.

Get away from the presence of a fool;
you will not meet knowing lips there.

The wisdom of the shrewd is to understand his road,
but the folly of fools is deceit.

Fools make a joke of guilt,{c}
but among the upright there is goodwill.

Only the heart knows its bitter places,
and in its gladness no outsider has a share.

The house of the wicked will be wiped out,
but the tent of the upright will flourish.

There is a road that looks straight to a man,
but at its end are the roads of death.

A heart can hurt while it laughs,
and joy may finish in sorrow.

The backslider gets his fill of his own ways,
and a good man, of what is his.{d}

The naive believes every word,
but the shrewd watches his steps.

The wise is cautious and turns away from evil,
but the fool is reckless and sure of himself.

The quick-tempered does foolish things,
and a schemer is hated.

The naive inherit folly,
but the shrewd are crowned with knowledge.

The evil bow down before the good,
and the wicked at the gates of the righteous.

The poor man is disliked even by his neighbor,
but the rich have friends by the dozen.

Whoever despises his neighbor sins,
but happy is the one who is kind to the poor.

Do not those who plot evil go astray?
Those who plan good meet with loyalty and faithfulness.

Every kind of toil yields a gain;
talk of the lips brings only lack.

The crown of the wise is their riches;
the folly of fools is folly.{e}

A witness who tells the truth delivers lives;
a witness who puffs out lies is fraud itself.

In the fear of Yahweh there is strong confidence,
and his children will have a refuge.

The fear of Yahweh is a fountain of life,
for turning aside from the snares of death.

A king’s glory lies in a multitude of people,
but without people a prince is ruined.

The patient person has great understanding,
but the quick-tempered puts folly on display.

A calm heart gives life to the body,
but envy is rot in the bones.

Whoever oppresses the poor insults his Maker,
but whoever is gracious to the needy honors him.

The wicked is thrown down by his own evil,
but the righteous finds refuge even in his death.{f}

In a discerning heart Wisdom settles down to rest;
inside fools she is made known.{g}

Righteousness lifts a nation high,
but sin is a disgrace to any people.

The king favors a servant who acts wisely,
but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully.

notes.text: Or “Wisdom builds her house,” reading the plural as an honorific, as in 9:1.
Or “a shoot of pride.”
Or “Guilt mocks fools.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Or “and a good man, from what he does.”
The Septuagint reads “a shrewd man is the crown of the wise, but the occupation of fools is evil.”
Hebrew bemoto. Many interpreters read betummo, “in his integrity,” by transposing two letters; the Septuagint has “in his own holiness.”
The Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read “but in the heart of fools she is not known.”

verses.text:
A gentle answer turns back rage,
but a word that wounds stirs up anger.

Knowledge sounds good from a wise tongue;
folly bubbles from the mouths of fools.

The eyes of Yahweh are everywhere,
watching the evil and the good.

A healing tongue is a tree of life,
but a twisted one crushes the spirit.

A fool spurns his father’s discipline,
but whoever accepts correction shows good sense.

In the house of the righteous there is great treasure,
but trouble comes with the earnings of the wicked.

The lips of the wise scatter knowledge,
but not so the heart of fools.

The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to Yahweh,
but the prayer of the upright is his delight.

The road of the wicked is loathsome to Yahweh;
the one who chases after righteousness he loves.

Harsh discipline awaits the one who leaves the path;
whoever hates correction will die.

Sheol and Abaddon{a} lie open before Yahweh;
how much more human hearts!

A mocker does not like to be corrected;
he will not go to the wise.

A glad heart makes a cheerful face,
but by heartache the spirit is crushed.

The discerning heart seeks knowledge,
but the mouth of fools grazes on folly.

Every day is a hard day for the poor,
but a good heart feasts without end.

Better a little with the fear of Yahweh
than great treasure and turmoil with it.

Better a dish of vegetables where there is love
than a fattened ox and hatred with it.

A hot-tempered man stirs up conflict,
but one slow to anger calms a quarrel.{b}

The way of the sluggard is like a hedge of thorns,
but the path of the upright is a highway.

A wise son makes a father glad,
but a foolish man despises his mother.

Foolishness pleases the senseless;
the discerning keeps a straight course.

Where no one takes counsel, plans come apart;
where advisers are many, they hold.

A person finds joy in an apt reply,
and a word in season, how good it is!

For the wise the path of life leads upward,
so that he turns away from Sheol below.

Yahweh tears down the house of the proud,
but he sets the widow’s boundary in place.

Evil plans are detestable to Yahweh,
but kind words are pure.

A man grasping after profit brings trouble home;
a man who hates a gift will live.{c}

The heart of the righteous weighs its answers,
but the mouth of the wicked gushes out evil.{d}

Yahweh is far from the wicked,
but he hears the prayer of the righteous.{e}

Bright eyes gladden the heart;
good news puts fat on the bones.

The ear that listens to life-giving correction
will lodge among the wise.{f}

To shrug off discipline is to reject your own life;
to hear reproof is to acquire a heart.

Fear of Yahweh trains a person in wisdom,
and lowliness walks ahead of glory.

notes.text: Abaddon, “destruction,” is a name for the realm of the dead, paired with Sheol.
The Septuagint adds “A man slow to anger will put out quarrels, but an ungodly man stirs them up instead.”
The Septuagint adds “By almsgiving and faithful dealing sins are cleansed away, but by the fear of the Lord everyone turns from evil,” a form of 16:6.
The Septuagint adds “The ways of righteous people are acceptable to the Lord, and through them even enemies become friends,” a form of 16:7.

The Septuagint adds “Better a small income with righteousness than abundant produce with unrighteousness. Let a person’s heart think rightly, so that his steps may be made straight by God,” forms of 16:8–9.
The Septuagint lacks this verse.

verses.text:
The plans of the heart belong to a person,
but the answer of the tongue comes from Yahweh.{a}

All a man’s ways are pure in his own eyes,
but Yahweh weighs the spirits.

Roll your works onto Yahweh,
and your plans will be established.

Yahweh has made everything for its own end,
even the wicked for the day of disaster.

Everyone proud of heart is detestable to Yahweh;
be sure of it, he will not go unpunished.

By loyal love and faithfulness guilt is atoned for,
and by the fear of Yahweh one turns away from evil.

When Yahweh is pleased with a man’s ways,
he makes even his enemies be at peace with him.

Better a little with righteousness
than large revenues without justice.

A man’s heart plans his way,
but Yahweh directs his steps.

An oracle is on the lips of a king;
his mouth must not betray justice.

Honest balance and scales belong to Yahweh;
all the weights in the bag are his work.

Doing evil is detestable to kings,
for a throne is made firm by righteousness.

Kings take pleasure in honest lips;
they love a straight talker.

A king’s wrath is a messenger of death,
but a wise man will appease it.

In the light of a king’s face is life,
and his favor is like a cloud bringing the spring rain.

How much better to get wisdom than gold!
To get understanding is to be chosen over silver.

The highway of the upright turns away from evil;
whoever watches his way guards his life.

Pride goes before destruction,
and a haughty spirit before a fall.

Better to be humble in spirit with the lowly
than to divide plunder with the proud.

Whoever pays attention to a matter will find good,
and happy is the one who trusts in Yahweh.

The wise of heart is called discerning,
and sweet speech adds persuasiveness.

Insight is a spring of life to its owner;
folly is the fool’s own punishment.

The heart of the wise makes his mouth prudent
and adds persuasiveness to his lips.

Pleasant words are a honeycomb,
sweet to the soul and healing to the bones.

There is a road that looks straight to a man,
but at its end are the roads of death.

A laborer’s appetite works for him,
for his mouth urges him on.

A worthless man digs up evil,
and on his lips it is like a scorching fire.

A perverse man spreads strife,
and a whisperer separates close friends.

A violent man entices his neighbor
and leads him in a way that is not good.

Whoever winks his eyes is plotting perversity;
whoever purses his lips has finished his evil.

Gray hair is a crown of glory;
it is found in the way of righteousness.

Better one slow to anger than a warrior,
and one who rules his spirit than one who takes a city.

The lot is thrown into the lap,
but every decision from it comes from Yahweh.

notes.text: The Septuagint lacks verses 1, 3, 4, and 6 in this form; forms of verses 6–9 also appear at the end of chapter 15.

verses.text:
A dry crust eaten in quiet
beats a house full of feasting{a} with quarrels.

A servant with good sense will rule over a son who brings shame
and share the inheritance with the brothers.

The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold,
but Yahweh is the tester of hearts.

An evildoer listens closely to wicked lips;
a liar lends his ear to a ruinous tongue.

To mock the poor is to insult the one who made them;
the person glad at disaster will not escape punishment.

Grandchildren are the crown of the old,
and parents are the pride of their children.{b}

Fine speech does not suit a fool,
still less lying lips a noble.

A bribe is a lucky stone in its owner’s eyes;
wherever he turns, it brings success.

To cover an offense is to seek love;
to keep bringing it up splits close friends.

A reprimand sinks further into someone with discernment
than a hundred lashes into a fool.

Rebellion is all an evil man is after;
a merciless envoy will be dispatched to deal with him.

Meet a bear robbed of her cubs
rather than a fool in his folly.

If someone pays back evil for good,
evil will never leave his house.

Starting a quarrel is like letting out water;
so drop the matter before the dispute breaks out.

Acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent—
Yahweh detests both alike.

What good is money in a fool’s hand
to buy wisdom, when he has no mind for it?{c}

A friend loves at all times,
and a brother is born for the hard times.

A man without sense strikes hands in pledge
and puts up security for his neighbor.

The lover of offense is a lover of strife;
whoever builds his gate high is asking for a fall.

One crooked of heart finds no good,
and one with a twisted tongue falls into trouble.

Whoever fathers a fool gets grief,
and the father of a dolt has no joy.

A glad heart is good medicine,
but a broken spirit dries up the bones.

A wicked man takes a bribe from under his cloak{d}
to bend the paths of justice.

The discerning keeps wisdom in view,
but the eyes of a fool roam to the ends of the earth.

A foolish son is a vexation to his father
and bitterness to the woman who bore him.

To fine the innocent is not good,
nor to flog nobles for their uprightness.

Whoever holds back his words has knowledge,
and the cool of spirit is a person of understanding.

Even a fool who keeps silent is counted wise;
with closed lips he passes for discerning.

notes.text: Literally “sacrifices,” since meat was eaten at sacrificial meals.
The Septuagint adds “The faithful have a whole world of wealth, but the faithless not even a penny.”
The Septuagint adds “Whoever makes his own house high seeks ruin, and whoever turns aside from learning will fall into trouble.”
Literally “from the bosom,” the fold of the garment.

verses.text:
One who separates himself pursues his own desire;
he bursts out against all sound judgment.{a}

A fool takes no pleasure in understanding,
only in airing his own opinions.

When wickedness arrives, contempt comes too,
and with dishonor comes reproach.

The words of a man’s mouth are deep waters,
the spring of wisdom a flowing stream.

It is not good to favor the guilty
or to push aside the innocent in court.

The lips of a fool march him into strife;
his mouth begs for blows.

A fool’s mouth is his ruin,
and his lips are a snare to his life.

The words of a whisperer are like tasty morsels;
they go down into the inner rooms of the belly.

Whoever is slack in his work
is brother to the one who destroys.

The name of Yahweh is a strong tower;
the righteous runs into it and is set high and safe.

A rich man’s wealth is his strong city,
and in his imagination it is like a high wall.

Before ruin a man’s heart grows proud,
and humility comes before honor.

Whoever answers before he has heard
shows his folly and his shame.

A person’s spirit can bear his sickness,
but a crushed spirit—who can carry it?

The discerning heart acquires knowledge,
and the ear of the wise searches it out.

A man’s gift opens the way for him
and brings him before the great.

The first to state his case seems right,
until the other side comes and questions him.

The lot puts an end to disputes
and settles things between the powerful.

A brother offended is harder to win than a strong city,
and quarrels are like the bars of a fortress.{b}

From the fruit of a man’s mouth his belly is filled;
he is filled with the yield of his lips.

Death and life are in the power of the tongue,
and those who love it will eat its fruit.

He who finds a wife finds a good thing
and obtains favor from Yahweh.{c}

The poor man speaks in pleading tones,
but the rich man answers roughly.{d}

A man of many companions may come to ruin,
but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.

notes.text: The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.
The Septuagint adds “Whoever puts away a good wife puts away a good thing, and whoever keeps an adulteress is foolish and ungodly.”
The Septuagint lacks verses 23–24 and 19:1–2.

verses.text:
Better a poor man walking in his integrity
than one with twisted lips who is a fool.

Desire without knowledge is not good,
and whoever hurries with his feet misses the way.

A man’s own folly ruins his way,
and his heart rages against Yahweh.

Wealth adds many friends,
but the poor man is deserted by his friend.

The liar on the witness stand will be held guilty;
whoever puffs out falsehoods will not get away.

Many court the favor of a generous man,
and everyone is a friend to a man who gives gifts.

Whoever gets sense loves his own life;
whoever keeps understanding will find good.

The liar on the witness stand will be held guilty;
whoever puffs out falsehoods will perish.

Luxury does not suit a fool,
still less a slave ruling over princes.

A person’s good sense makes him slow to anger,
and it is his glory to overlook an offense.

A king’s rage is like a lion’s roar,
but his favor is like dew on the grass.

A stupid son brings disaster on his father,
and a nagging wife is a roof that leaks without stopping.

A house and riches come down from one’s ancestors;
a wife with insight is Yahweh’s gift.

Laziness casts into a deep sleep,
and an idle person will go hungry.

Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life;
whoever is careless of his ways will die.

Whoever is kind to the poor lends to Yahweh,
and he will repay him for his deed.

Train your son while hope remains;
do not lift your soul toward putting him to death.{b}

A man of great wrath will pay the penalty;
if you rescue him, you will have to do it again.

Hear counsel, take correction,
and in the end you will be wise.

Many are the plans in a man’s heart,
but it is Yahweh’s purpose that will stand.

What is desired in a person is loyal love,{c}
and a poor man is better than a liar.

The fear of Yahweh leads to life;
one has it and rests content, untouched by harm.

The lazy man plunges his hand into the bowl
and is too tired to lift it back to his lips.

Strike a mocker, and the naive will learn shrewdness;
correct a discerning person, and he will gain knowledge.

Whoever robs his father and drives out his mother
is a son who brings shame and disgrace.

Stop listening to discipline, my son,
and you will stray from words of knowledge.

A worthless witness mocks at justice,
and the mouth of the wicked swallows iniquity.

Judgments are ready for mockers,
and beatings for the backs of fools.

notes.text: The third line is uncertain; it may be a fragment of a lost saying. The Septuagint has a longer text here.
Or “do not set your heart on causing him to die,” that is, do not discipline in rage; or “do not let your heart be set on ruining him” by neglect.
Or “A person’s greed is his shame.”

verses.text:
Wine is a scoffer, strong drink a brawler;
no one led astray by it is wise.

A king’s fury is like the growl of a young lion;
whoever angers him forfeits his life.

It is to a man’s credit to keep clear of strife,
but every fool bares his teeth.

The lazy man does not plow when autumn comes;
at harvest he looks for a crop and there is none.

The purpose in a person’s heart is deep water,
but a discerning person will draw it up.

Many a man proclaims his own loyalty,
but a faithful man—who can find one?

The righteous walks on in his integrity;
happy are his children after him!

A king seated on the throne of judgment
sifts out all evil with his eyes.

Who can say, “I have made my heart clean;
I am pure from my sin”?{a}

Two kinds of weights and two kinds of measures{b}—
Yahweh detests both of them.

Even a child makes himself known by his acts,
whether his conduct is pure and upright.

A listening ear, a seeing eye—
Yahweh is the maker of the pair.

Do not love sleep, or you will be poor;
keep your eyes open and you will have your fill of bread.

“Bad, bad,” says the buyer,
but when he goes off, then he boasts.{c}

There is gold and plenty of coral,
but lips with knowledge are the rarest jewel.

Take the garment of one who stands surety for a stranger;
hold it as a pledge when he guarantees a foreign woman.{d}

Food got by cheating tastes sweet at first,
but later the mouth is crammed with grit.

Plans are made firm by taking counsel;
wage war with sound guidance.

A gossip goes around revealing secrets,
so do not mix with someone whose lips are always open.

Whoever curses his father or his mother,
his lamp will go out in deepest darkness.

An inheritance seized in haste at the start
will not be blessed in the end.

Do not say, “I will pay back evil”;
wait for Yahweh, and he will rescue you.

Two kinds of weights are detestable to Yahweh,
and false scales are not good.

A man’s steps are from Yahweh;
how then can a person understand his own way?

It is a snare to blurt out, “Holy!”
and only afterward to think over one’s vows.

A wise king winnows the wicked
and drives the threshing wheel over them.

The human spirit is the lamp of Yahweh,
searching all the inner rooms of the belly.

Loyal love and faithfulness guard a king,
and by loyal love he holds up his throne.

The glory of young men is their strength,
and the splendor of the old is gray hair.

Blows that wound scour away evil,
and beatings reach the inner rooms of the belly.

notes.text: In the Septuagint verses 20–22 follow here, and verses 14–19 are absent.
Literally “a stone and a stone, an ephah and an ephah,” that is, one set of weights and measures for buying and another for selling. The ephah was a dry measure of about 3/5 bushel (22 liters).
The Septuagint lacks verses 14–19.
Or “a foreigner,” following another reading of the Hebrew; compare 27:13.

verses.text:
A king’s heart is a stream of water in Yahweh’s hand;
he turns it wherever he pleases.

Every way a man takes is right in his own eyes,
but Yahweh weighs hearts.

Doing righteousness and justice
pleases Yahweh better than sacrifice.

Haughty eyes and a proud heart—
the lamp of the wicked is sin.{a}

The plans of the diligent lead only to profit,
but everyone who is hasty comes only to want.{b}

Treasures gained by a lying tongue
are a vanishing vapor, snares of death.{c}

The violence of the wicked will sweep them away,
because they refuse to do what is just.

The way of a guilty man is crooked,
but the conduct of the pure is upright.

Better a spot on a corner of the rooftop
than a whole house with a contentious woman.

The soul of the wicked craves evil;
his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes.

When a mocker is punished, the naive becomes wise;
when the wise is instructed, he gains knowledge.

The Righteous One{d} takes note of the wicked man’s house
and hurls the wicked into disaster.

Whoever shuts his ear to the cry of the poor
will himself cry out and not be answered.

A gift in secret soothes anger,
and a bribe in the cloak, strong wrath.

Justice carried out delights the righteous
and terrifies those who do wrong.

A person who strays off the road of insight
will end up resting among the company of the shades.

Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man;
whoever loves wine and oil will not grow rich.

The wicked is a ransom for the righteous,
and the treacherous for the upright.

Better to live in a desert land
than with a quarrelsome and fretful wife.

Precious treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the wise,
but a foolish man swallows them up.

Whoever pursues righteousness and loyal love
finds life, righteousness, and honor.

A wise man goes up against a city of warriors
and brings down the stronghold they trusted.

Keep watch on mouth and tongue,
and you keep your soul out of distress.

“Mocker” is the name of the proud and arrogant man
who acts with insolent pride.

The craving of the sluggard kills him,
for his hands refuse to work.

He spends the whole day longing for more;
the righteous man gives without stinting.

The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable,
how much more when he brings it with evil intent!

A lying witness will perish,
but a man who listens will speak to the end.{e}

The wicked man hardens his face;
the upright man makes his ways sure.{f}

There is no wisdom, no understanding,
no counsel against Yahweh.

They harness the horse for the day of war,
yet the victory is Yahweh’s.

notes.text: Or “the tillage of the wicked”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
The Septuagint lacks this verse.
So the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses; the Hebrew reads “for those who seek death.”
Or “A righteous man”; the subject of the second line suggests God.
Or “will speak successfully”; the meaning is uncertain.
So the Masoretic marginal reading; the written text has “understands his ways.”

verses.text:
A good name is to be chosen over great riches;
favor is better than silver and gold.

Rich and poor meet together;
Yahweh is the Maker of them all.

The shrewd sees trouble and hides,
but the naive go on and pay for it.

The reward of humility and the fear of Yahweh
is riches and honor and life.

Thorns and snares lie in the way of the crooked;
whoever guards his life keeps far from them.

Train a child in keeping with his way;
even when he is old he will not turn from it.{a}

The rich rules over the poor,
and the borrower is slave to the lender.

Whoever sows injustice will reap trouble,
and the rod of his fury will fail.{b}

The generous will be blessed,
for he shares his bread with the poor.{c}

Drive out the mocker and strife goes out;
quarreling and insult will stop.

One who loves a pure heart and has grace on his lips
will win the king’s friendship.

The eyes of Yahweh watch over knowledge,
but he overturns the words of the treacherous.

The sluggard says, “There is a lion outside!
I will be killed in the streets!”

The mouth of foreign women is a deep pit;
the one under Yahweh’s anger will fall into it.{d}

Folly is bound up in the heart of a boy;
the rod of discipline will drive it far from him.

Grinding down the poor to enrich oneself,
giving presents to the rich—both end in want.

Turn your ear and hear the words of the wise,{e}
and set your heart on my knowledge,

for it is pleasant if you keep them within you,
if all of them are ready on your lips.

So that your trust may be in Yahweh,
I have made them known to you today, even to you.

See, I have written down for you thirty{f}
of counsel and knowledge,

to teach you what is right and true, words that can be relied on,
so that you can bring back a true answer to those who sent you?

Do not plunder a poor man just because he is poor,
and do not trample the lowly in the gate,

for Yahweh will plead their case
and rob of life those who rob them.

Do not befriend a hot-tempered man,
or go around with a man of rage,

or you will learn his ways
and get yourself caught in a snare.

Do not be one of those who strike hands in pledge,
who stand as security for debts.

If you have nothing to pay with,
why should your bed be taken from under you?

Do not move the ancient boundary stone
that your fathers set up.

You see a man who is quick and expert at his trade?
Before kings he will take his place,
not before men of no account.

notes.text: Or “according to the way he should go.” The Septuagint lacks this verse.
The Septuagint adds “God loves a cheerful and generous man, but he will bring the emptiness of his works to an end”; compare 2 Corinthians 9:7.
The Septuagint adds “Whoever gives freely wins victory and honor, but he takes away the life of those who possess them.”
The Septuagint adds “Evil ways lie before a man, and he does not like to turn from them, but he must turn aside from a twisted and evil way.”
A new collection begins here (22:17–24:22), with close parallels in the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, which is divided into thirty chapters.

So the Masoretic marginal reading, as many interpreters understand it; the written text reads shilshom, “formerly,” and the marginal reading shalishim is also taken as “excellent things.” The Septuagint reads “record them for yourself three times.”
